newsitem.title: ROMANIA: East Europe's NATO also-rans seek early admission.
newsitem.headline: East Europe's NATO also-rans seek early admission.

text.p: Led by Romania and Slovakia, East European countries widely considered to be also-rans in the stakes to win NATO membership have launched campaigns to persuade the alliance to let them in the first expansion wave.

NATO is likely to decide some time next year which former communist states to draw into its movement eastward and conventional thinking has made Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia the favourites.
The outsiders, fearing that exclusion would leave them in a no-man's-land between the West and a suspicious Russia, have made known that they are taking no such decision for granted.
Romanian Foreign Minister Teodor Melescanu has led a phalanx of emissaries fanning out across Europe and North America with President Ion Iliescu's plea for quick entry.

"We thought it appropriate to reiterate our bid to join NATO and our arguments for quick admission now, when NATO countries are preparing a decision on new members," Iliescu's spokesman, Traian Chebeleu, told a news conference on Thursday.
Slovakia's Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik told the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna that quick admission was vital for national interests.

"The Slovak Republic still finds itself in...an inconvenient and historically risky security vacuum," he said. "We do not want to be a bridge to the East...The Slovak Republic has an eminent interest in joining NATO in the first wave..."
The former Yugoslav republic of Slovenia, seen by many as a better bet for early membership, received a boost from a two-day NATO steering committee meeting in Ljubljana.
Deputy Secretary General Sergio Balanzino praised Slovenia's military development and said membership would pose no problems for NATO's ties with Russia.

The second line of prospective entrants will be keeping an eye on just how virulent Russia will be in opposing expansion -- though all, including Ukraine on its southern flank, say Moscow cannot veto any country's membership bid.
Russia's top security official, Alexander Lebed, reiterated on Thursday Moscow's old reluctance to NATO's planned eastward drive, after appearing more amenable during talks in Brussels.

Even the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, part of the Soviet Union a mere five years ago, still harbour hopes of joining quickly, though Moscow is particularly upset about their membership aspirations.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, speaking in Denmark after a 13-nation naval exercise including the Baltic states, said no country had been ruled out in granting new memberships.
Diplomats said there was no certainty that the four favourites were by any means shoo-ins.
"The Romanians are certainly going about this the right way by drawing attention to their case and improving what has sometimes been a negative image abroad," said a Bucharest-based Western diplomat.
"Some countries have been more aggressive than others in promoting themselves. But many may not in fact want membership now. Bulgaria is a prime case."

Bulgaria is torn between an anti-leftist opposition which wants to anchor Sofia inside NATO and the ruling socialists eager to avoid upsetting Russia. The country is focussing on economic crisis and this month's presidential elections.
Albania, a keen participant in NATO's Partnership for Peace cooperation programme, appears more enthusiastic but willing to wait for subsequent membership drives.

Ukraine has perhaps the most delicate position. It is seeking a "special partnership" with NATO instead of outright membership. It has also sought assurances that no nuclear weapons will be deployed in new member states.
